llm.summary: This is a documentation-only hook-authoring skill, but it repeatedly teaches broad logging, external hook calls, and prompt/context injection without enough privacy boundaries.

dimensions.detail: The stated purpose is security-first hook authoring, and most capabilities are purpose-aligned, but examples include posting full hook input to HTTP endpoints, logging raw tool input, and injecting project files into prompts without adjacent privacy controls.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The guidance covers plugin, project, and global hooks, including always-on global settings and automatically loaded plugin hooks; several examples are broad enough to affect all sessions or all tool inputs.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The artifact contains Markdown skill documentation and modules only, with no executable hook files, package dependencies, or install-time code; static scan was clean and VirusTotal telemetry was absent.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Hook authoring naturally involves local files, commands, network calls, and automation, but the examples sometimes normalize outbound requests, raw input capture, and cross-project behavior without clear scoping or consent guidance.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill teaches persistent audit logs, background log writers, durable scheduled tasks, and global hook configuration; these are disclosed as concepts but not consistently bounded for sensitive prompts, secrets, or retention.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Review before installing or using this skill to generate hooks. Prefer its validation and sanitization patterns, but do not copy examples that send full hook payloads to external services, log raw CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT, persist prompts, or emit rm -rf cleanup commands unless you add explicit consent, allowlists, redaction, retention limits, and trusted endpoints.
llm.findings:
[SQP-2] expected: HTTP hook support is expected for hook authoring, but the example confirms a full standard hook payload can be posted to a URL without an adjacent warning about sensitive prompts, paths, and tool inputs.
[SQP-2] expected: The hook-types module repeats the HTTP hook data flow; this supports a privacy under-disclosure concern, not a finding that the skill itself exfiltrates data.
[SQP-2] expected: Durable cron persistence is described accurately, but the documentation does not clearly warn that scheduled prompts may be stored on disk.
[SQP-2] unexpected: The observability module recommends copy-pasteable deletion commands including an rm -rf example; it is framed narrowly, but this is risky guidance for an automation skill.
[SQP-2] expected: Performance examples persist tool names, timestamps, and sizes; this is normal telemetry, but the broader logging guidance lacks consistent privacy and retention warnings.
[SQP-2] expected: Remote config and logging examples are purpose-aligned, but they do not consistently require TLS, metadata minimization, or explicit review before sending operational data.
[SQP-2] unexpected: The global audit example logs CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT directly to a persistent file, which is overbroad because tool input may contain secrets, paths, prompts, or proprietary data.
[SQP-2] expected: SDK audit logging is mostly bounded and includes sanitization, so this concern is downgraded, though users still need retention and file-permission guidance.
[SQP-2] expected: Context injection from README, conventions, and architecture files is plausible for hook examples, but the pattern should be opt-in and filtered because it can expose private project content to prompts.
